Repo: C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Windows paths, Git-Bash/PowerShell environment). Kodely, an AI website builder. No new npm dependencies allowed (this is about static font FILES, not packages).

BACKGROUND: Generated sites currently all look "generic" per direct user feedback. Two root causes were diagnosed by reading lib/agent.ts:
1. Every single generated site is locked to the exact same system font stack (line ~70 of lib/agent.ts: "Fonts come from the system stack... No @font-face — not even with a base64 data: URI"). Zero typographic variation across the entire product.
2. The only anti-genericness instruction is one soft sentence ("give the page one distinctive visual idea rather than a generic hero-plus-three-cards") with no concrete mechanism — no forced design-decision step, no explicit list of the AI-generated-design clichés to avoid.

YOUR JOB has two parts. Read lib/agent.ts in full, and app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts + app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts (the SANDBOX_CSP constant exists in BOTH and the comment in the site route explicitly says they "MUST STAY IN SYNC" — if you change one, change both identically) before touching anything.

## PART 1 — Self-hosted fonts

**Step 1, verify before assuming:** The current CSP is `default-src 'self'; ...; connect-src 'none'; ...` with no explicit `font-src` directive. Per the CSP spec, an unset `font-src` falls back to `default-src`. The comment in lib/agent.ts says "The CSP sets no font-src, so fonts fall back to default-src 'self', which does NOT allow data: ... A base64 font is blocked exactly like a hosted one" — but this claim needs verification specifically for a REAL same-origin file request (not a data: URI), because `default-src 'self'` conceptually SHOULD permit a normal same-origin GET request for any resource type, unlike a `data:` URI which is a different scheme `'self'` doesn't cover. Do not just trust the existing comment or my restatement of it — actually verify empirically: build a minimal real test (e.g. use the preview pipeline or a small standalone reproduction serving the exact SANDBOX_CSP header alongside a real same-origin .woff2 file reference in a @font-face rule) and check in a real browser (via the browser tool available to you) whether the font actually loads or a CSP violation is reported in the console/network tab. Base your decision on what you actually observe, not on assumption. If a same-origin real font file IS blocked under the current CSP, add `font-src 'self'` to BOTH SANDBOX_CSP constants (site route and preview route) identically, and update the comment in lib/agent.ts to describe the corrected reality. If same-origin file loading turns out to already work fine (only base64 data: URIs are blocked), do NOT touch the CSP at all — just update the incorrect/misleading part of the lib/agent.ts comment to be accurate, and proceed with real hosted files (never base64) for the rest of this task.

**Step 2, source real font files.** Pull a small curated set (3–4 pairings is enough — this is meant to give real variety, not become a font library) of open-source webfonts from Google Fonts' official GitHub repository (github.com/google/fonts) — every font there is under a real open license (SIL Open Font License, or occasionally Apache 2.0); verify the specific `OFL.txt` (or `LICENSE.txt`) file exists in that font's own directory in that repo before including it, and keep a copy of that license file locally alongside the fonts you vendor (a `licenses/` or per-family `LICENSE` file — do not vendor a font without its license text). Suggested starting candidates (verify licensing yourself, swap any that don't check out): a genuinely distinctive serif display face for an editorial/warm look (e.g. Fraunces), a geometric sans for a modern/technical look (e.g. Space Grotesk), a warm rounded sans for a friendly/approachable look (e.g. Nunito or Baloo 2), and one clean, highly-legible body sans distinct from the system stack to pair with whichever display face needs one (e.g. Work Sans or Public Sans). For each family, only fetch the weights actually needed (typically 400/500/600/700 — do not vendor every available weight), in WOFF2 format only (smallest, universally supported by every browser this product needs to support). Keep the total vendored size modest — a few hundred KB per family, roughly 1–3MB total is the target ballpark; if your selections balloon past that, trim weights or swap a lighter-weight family.

**Step 3, get the files into every generated site's actual served output.** Read lib/foundation.ts and lib/build-site.ts to understand how a new project's starting file tree is seeded and how the Vite build produces the served output (note: Vite copies a `public/` directory verbatim into the build output — this is almost certainly the simplest real mechanism: seed every project's `public/fonts/` directory with all the vendored font files as part of project foundation, so they always exist in the build output at a predictable same-origin path like `/fonts/<family>-<weight>.woff2`, and the AI just references whichever ones it actually uses via `@font-face`. Confirm this Vite `public/` behavior against how this project's actual build step is configured (check the Vite config it generates/uses) before committing to this approach — use whatever mechanism this codebase's actual build pipeline genuinely supports.
Confirm the site-serving GET route can actually serve `.woff2` (check the MIME map in app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts — it may already list `woff2: "font/woff2"`; if so that's a promising sign this was anticipated, verify it actually gets exercised correctly end-to-end for a real file).

## PART 2 — Force real design decisions, name the clichés to avoid

Rewrite the "## Quality bar" section of lib/agent.ts (and the font-rule paragraph from Part 1) to require an actual short design-plan step before the model writes any markup, not just a soft aspiration. Specifically:

1. Before generating page content, the model must commit to: a real palette (named as 4–6 actual hex values, not "a warm palette"), ONE of the curated font pairings from Part 1 chosen deliberately for a stated reason (a sentence connecting the choice to the specific business/subject — e.g. "a bakery run by hand for 20 years reads better in a warm serif than a geometric sans"), and a one-sentence layout concept for how this specific business's content will be organized (not necessarily unconventional, just deliberate and stated).
2. Add an explicit list of AI-generated-design defaults to actively AVOID unless the brief specifically calls for one of them: warm cream background with a serif display and a terracotta/rust accent; near-black background with a single neon-green or vermilion accent pop; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on a white page; centering every single element; `rounded-lg` (or equivalent) applied uniformly to every card with no variation; emoji used as section markers/bullets; an accent-color vertical bar/rail as the only visual distinguishor on otherwise-identical cards. State plainly that landing on one of these by genuine deliberate choice for a specific brief is fine — the instruction is against defaulting to them unthinkingly on every single build.
3. Keep the existing real, load-bearing constraints from the current quality-bar section intact (real specific copy never invented facts about a real business, responsive to 380px, semantic HTML, focus states, dark-mode treatment) — you are STRENGTHENING this section's design-decision rigor, not removing its existing honesty/accessibility requirements.

## Constraints
- Do not change anything about the NOT_OFFERED features list in lib/features.ts, the SiteRecord/accounts work from prior phases, or any unrelated part of the CSP beyond exactly what Part 1's verification concludes is needed.
- Do not add any new npm dependency — vendored font files are static assets, not packages.
- Do not touch app/admin/ or anything outside the generation pipeline / CSP / asset-serving path.

## Verification
Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean. Additionally, if feasible without spending significant model-generation credits, verify at least once end-to-end that a real generated/preview page can actually load one of the vendored fonts under the real CSP header (reuse the preview pipeline rather than running a full paid build if there's a cheaper way to exercise the same serving path) — describe exactly what you checked and observed.

Report back: what your empirical CSP test found (did font-src need to change or not, and why), the exact font families/weights/licenses you vendored and their total size, how the files get into every project's actual served output, and the exact new quality-bar text you wrote into lib/agent.ts.

81	/**
82	 * Which stored build file answers a requested URL path.
83	 *
84	 * Generated sites are multi-page (lib/foundation.ts): `vite build` emits a real
85	 * document per page — index.html, about.html, blog/index.html — and visitors
86	 * ask for /about, not /about.html. This is the whole server-side cost of that.
87	 *
88	 * Deliberately NOT the SPA catch-all ("serve index.html for anything unknown").
89	 * That shape is what a client-side router needs, and it turns every typo, every
90	 * dead inbound link and every stale crawl URL into a 200 serving the home page —
91	 * soft 404s, which Google treats as a quality problem on the whole site. Here a
92	 * path resolves only to a file that actually exists under one of two well-known
93	 * spellings, and everything else still 404s exactly as it did before.
94	 *
95	 * Anything carrying an extension resolves to itself and nothing else, which is
96	 * what keeps robots.txt, sitemap.xml and /assets/* on their existing single
97	 * path — no candidate list can shadow them.
98	 */
99	function candidatePaths(filePath: string): string[] {
100	  if (/\.[A-Za-z0-9]+$/.test(filePath)) return [filePath];
101	  const clean = filePath.replace(/\/+$/, "");
102	  if (!clean) return ["index.html"];
103	  // Order matters: about.html wins over about/index.html when a site has both.
104	  return [`${clean}.html`, `${clean}/index.html`];
105	}

262	          baseUrl,
263	          pageUrl: pageUrl(baseUrl, file.path),

268	    headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME[ext] ?? "application/octet-stream" },

## Fonts — four real, self-hosted families, picked deliberately per site
Every project starts with four real webfont families already sitting in
\`public/fonts/\` — genuine .woff2 files, weights 400/500/600/700 each, seeded
into the project the same way every other foundation file is (lib/foundation.ts
via lib/foundation-fonts.ts). You never write a font file yourself; you only
reference the ones already there.

This works under the CSP because a real, same-origin file request is not what
the old version of this rule assumed. The CSP sets no \`font-src\`, so it falls
back to \`default-src 'self'\` — and \`'self'\` genuinely permits an ordinary
same-origin GET for any resource type, fonts included; this was verified
against a real browser loading a real .woff2 under this exact policy, not
assumed. What \`'self'\` does NOT cover is the \`data:\` scheme, which is why a
base64-embedded font is still blocked outright — never inline one. The same
logic blocks any remote host: no \`@import\`, no \`<link>\` to fonts.googleapis.com
or any other CDN, and no font file that isn't already one of the four below.

The four families, and the pairing each is meant for:
- **Fraunces** (\`/fonts/fraunces-{400,500,600,700}.woff2\`) — a distinctive
  serif display face. Reach for it when the subject reads as editorial, warm,
  or crafted: a bakery, a studio, a small hospitality brand, writing that
  wants some warmth in the letterforms themselves.
- **Space Grotesk** (\`/fonts/space-grotesk-{400,500,600,700}.woff2\`) — a
  geometric sans. Reach for it for anything that reads as modern or
  technical: software, a startup, a product, a service that wants to look
  precise rather than warm.
- **Baloo 2** (\`/fonts/baloo-2-{400,500,600,700}.woff2\`) — a warm, rounded
  sans. Reach for it when the brief is friendly and approachable rather than
  editorial or technical: kids' activities, community groups, casual food and
  drink, anything that should feel soft rather than sharp.
- **Work Sans** (\`/fonts/work-sans-{400,500,600,700}.woff2\`) — a clean,
  highly legible body sans, distinct from the system stack. This is the body
  copy partner for whichever of the three display faces above you pick; it is
  never the display face itself. (Space Grotesk and Baloo 2 can also carry
  their own short UI labels and buttons at 500/600 without switching to Work
  Sans, since both stay legible at body sizes — but paragraph copy should
  still be Work Sans.)

Pick exactly ONE display family for a build (see the Quality bar's design-plan
step below, which is where this choice actually gets made and justified) and
pair it with Work Sans for body text. Declare each weight you actually use as
its own \`@font-face\` rule in \`src/index.css\`, pointing at the real path —
e.g.:
\`\`\`css
@font-face {
  font-family: "Fraunces";
  src: url("/fonts/fraunces-700.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 700;
  font-display: swap;
}
\`\`\`
— then reference it with an ordinary Tailwind arbitrary value
(\`font-[Fraunces]\`) or by extending the theme. Declare only the weights you
actually use, not all four reflexively. If the system stack genuinely suits
the brief better than any of the four (rare, but possible for something that
wants to look plain/native rather than designed), that is a legitimate choice
too — the rule is against silently defaulting, not against ever choosing the
system stack on purpose.

### Commit to a design plan before writing any markup
Before you write the first component or page shell, decide and hold yourself
to three concrete things — not vague intentions, actual decisions you could
hand to another designer and have them build the same page:

1. **A real palette — 4 to 6 actual hex values.** Not "a warm palette" or "an
   earthy tone" — name the hex codes you're going to use for background,
   text, and accent(s) before you use them. Pick them for the subject, not
   from habit.
2. **One font pairing from the four families above, chosen for a stated
   reason.** Say, in one sentence, why this business or subject fits this
   pairing — "a bakery run by hand for 20 years reads better in a warm serif
   than a geometric sans," not just "using Fraunces." If the reason doesn't
   actually connect to the brief, the choice isn't done yet.
3. **A one-sentence layout concept for THIS content.** How is this specific
   business's material actually organised — not necessarily unconventional,
   just deliberate and stated: "a single long scrolling page built around the
   seasonal menu, since that's the one thing every visitor is here for," or
   "three service pages plus a shared quote-request footer, because pricing
   genuinely differs per service." A layout concept that would fit any
   business equally well is not a plan, it's a shrug.

Do this thinking before generating page content — it's what turns "give the
page one distinctive visual idea" from an aspiration into something you
actually did, on purpose, for this brief.

### Defaults to avoid, unless the brief genuinely calls for one
These are the shapes an AI-generated site reaches for when no real decision
got made. Landing on one of them BY GENUINE DELIBERATE CHOICE for a specific
brief is completely fine — a rustic bakery really might earn a warm cream
background and a serif face. What this rule is against is defaulting to one
of these unthinkingly, the same way, on every single build regardless of the
subject:
- Warm cream background + serif display face + a terracotta/rust accent.
- Near-black background with a single neon-green or vermilion accent as the
  only pop of colour.
- A purple-to-blue gradient hero sitting on an otherwise plain white page.
- Centering every single element on the page.
- \`rounded-lg\` (or an equivalent radius) applied uniformly to every card with
  no variation anywhere.
- Emoji used as section markers or bullet points.
- An accent-coloured vertical bar/rail as the only thing distinguishing
  otherwise-identical cards.

If you notice yourself reaching for one of these, ask whether it's because
the brief actually calls for it or because it's just the reflex — the design
plan above is what makes that distinction checkable instead of vibes.

### The load-bearing constraints, still fully in force
Real, specific copy for the subject at hand — never "Lorem ipsum" and never
placeholder headings like "Your Title Here". Responsive down to 380px.
Semantic HTML, labelled form controls, sufficient colour contrast, and a
visible :focus style. Include a dark-mode treatment unless the brief implies
otherwise. None of the design-decision rigor above replaces any of this —
it's stricter about the decisions, not looser about the honesty or
accessibility bar.
